title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
A Tesla vehicle with Autopilot engaged fatally crashed in 2024. Tesla told the family of the deceased that crash data from the vehicle did not exist. A security researcher recovered the data through Tesla's bug bounty program and demonstrated the data was present on the vehicle all along. The failure was a false statement to a family: Tesla asserted as fact that evidence was gone when the deployment system retained it.

The incident shows what happens when crash investigation depends on a single party's claim about what data exists. A jury found Tesla responsible and ordered damages. It is not established whether Tesla's statement about missing data resulted from system design, operational procedure, or other cause, or whether the company knew the data was recoverable when it made the statement to the family.

summary:
A lawsuit concluded in 2026 revealed that Tesla possessed crash data from a fatal accident in 2024 that killed Naibel Benavides Leon and injured Dillon Angulo, despite the company telling the grieving family the data was unavailable. A Russian hacker working through Tesla's bug bounty program recovered the missing crash footage and proved Tesla had access to it all along. A jury found Tesla partially responsible for the accident and ordered the company to pay 243 million dollars in damages, with the judge denying Tesla's appeal in February 2026.

The incident raises concerns about Tesla's transparency regarding its autonomous vehicle safety, as the company is preparing to launch fully self-driving Cybercabs. Recent data shows Tesla vehicles with driver-assist systems were involved in 207 crashes in May alone, the highest number on record. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating potential safety failures in Tesla's self-driving software, and reports suggest the company may have understated crash numbers to appear safer than it is.
